posts.title: Writing a will your family can actually read
posts.excerpt: Most of the estate disputes we see begin with a will that was valid but unclear. A few habits make a will easier to follow, and kinder to the people who have to carry it out.
posts.content:
A will has two readers. The first is the law, which asks whether it was made properly. The second is your family, who will read it at one of the hardest moments of their lives and try to work out what you meant. Most of the disputes we are asked to settle begin with a will that satisfied the first reader and confused the second.

Name things the way your family names them

“The house” may be obvious to you; to three children it may mean three different places. Describe property so that a stranger could find it, and people so that nobody has to guess: full names, and how they are related to you.

Say what happens if

Wills are often written for the world as it is today. Ask what should happen if someone named in it dies before you, if a property has been sold, or if the business has changed hands. A sentence for each is usually enough.

The kindest wills we read are short, specific and slightly boring.

Emi Shiro, founding partner

Keep a letter beside it

A will is not the place for explanations, but a separate letter can be. Many clients leave a page saying why they divided things as they did. It carries no legal weight, and it often prevents a great deal of hurt.

  • Review your will every five years, and after any marriage, divorce, birth or sale.
  • Tell your executor where the original is kept.
  • Consider a notarised will if your affairs are complicated or your family is not on speaking terms.

If you would like to talk through your own situation, a first consultation is a good place to start.

posts.title: Five clauses to reread in your shareholders' agreement
posts.excerpt: Founding agreements are signed in a hurry and filed for years. Five clauses are worth reading again once the company has grown up.
posts.content:
Most founders sign their shareholders' agreement in the same week as the company's registration, when there is more enthusiasm than time. Five years later the company has staff, customers and perhaps an investor, and the agreement still describes a kitchen table.

The five we look at first

  • Leaving. What happens to the shares of a founder who steps away, and at what price.
  • Deadlock. How decisions are made when two equal owners disagree.
  • New money. Whether existing owners can keep their share when new shares are issued.
  • Selling. Who must be asked first, and whether a buyer can force the others to sell too.
  • Death and illness. Whether shares pass to a family or back to the company.

None of these is difficult to fix while everyone is on good terms. All of them are very hard to fix afterwards.

An agreement is a letter to the people you will be in ten years. It helps if they can read it.

Ren Morita, associate

posts.title: Mediation first: how a family matter usually begins
posts.excerpt: Most separations we handle never reach a courtroom. Here is what mediation looks like in practice, and when it is not the right path.
posts.content:
When someone first comes to us about a separation, they often expect a fight. More often than not, what they need is a structured conversation, held somewhere calm, with someone in the room whose job is to keep it fair.

What happens in the room

Mediation sessions last about two hours. Both people attend, each with their own lawyer if they wish, and a trained mediator guides the conversation through money, the home and, above all, the children. Nothing agreed is binding until it is written down and signed.

When it is not the right path

Mediation depends on both people being able to speak freely. Where there has been violence or serious intimidation, we do not suggest it, and we move directly to protecting you through the family court.

A good agreement is one that both people can still live with in five years.

Takeshi Kanda, partner

posts.title: Before you print the label: a trademark check for makers
posts.excerpt: A name feels like yours the moment you choose it. A short check before the first print run can save a painful rebrand later.
posts.content:
Designers and small makers usually choose a name with care, and then print it on everything. The trouble starts when a letter arrives from someone who registered a similar name first, in the same class of goods.

A twenty-minute check

  • Search the public trademark register for the name and for close variations.
  • Check the classes of goods you sell now, and those you might sell in three years.
  • Look at how the name is used online, in shops and at markets in your field.

If the name is clear, filing an application is straightforward and not expensive. If it is not, it is far better to know before the first thousand labels are printed.

posts.title: Handing over the family company
posts.excerpt: Succession in a family business is part law, part tax and mostly conversation. Starting five years early is not too soon.
posts.content:
A family company passes to the next generation either by plan or by accident. The plan takes longer and is far kinder. It begins not with documents but with a question the owner rarely asks out loud: who, if anyone, wants to carry this on?

Three conversations before any paperwork

  • With the family: who wants to be involved, and who would rather be paid out fairly.
  • With the people who run the company day to day: who could lead it.
  • With the bank and the main customers: what they would need to hear.

The legal work, transferring shares, updating the articles and writing the wills to match, follows from those conversations. Done in that order, it is rarely the hardest part.

posts.title: Emi Shiro on writing contracts in plain language
posts.excerpt: A conversation with our founding partner about short sentences, long clauses and why the client should be able to read every word.
posts.content:
When Emi Shiro opened the office in 2009, she set one rule for every document that left it: the person who signs it should be able to read it without a lawyer beside them. We asked her how that has worked out.

Plain language is not simpler law. It is the same law, without the fog.

Emi Shiro

Does plain language make contracts less precise?

“Usually the opposite. Old phrases survive because nobody dares remove them, not because they are precise. When you rewrite a clause in plain words you find out whether it actually says anything.”

What is the hardest part?

“Resisting the temptation to sound like a lawyer. Clients are paying for judgment, not vocabulary.”
